\chapter{After You}
\label{ch:zh-qing}
\hlchaptermodality{11}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write \zh{请}, say it on its own to mean after you, explain that it invites rather than softens and so is used far less than English please, and I know a character half can point at the sound instead of the meaning.}

A complete courtesy in four words, and the point at which the reader learns a character can carry two kinds of hint at once -- one half for what it means, the other for how it sounds -- which is what makes the writing system learnable rather than thousands of unrelated pictures.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[qǐng]{\zh{请} — a half that tells you the sound}

\label{lesson:ZH-W11-qing}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{讠}. Dot, then one turning stroke. What does it tell you about the word? (\textbf{Speech}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\zh{请}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Ten strokes}, two pieces, and \zh{讠} is on the left again as you would expect.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{讠}} + \textbf{\zh{青}}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\zh{讠} (strokes 1-2).} Speech. You know it.

\textbf{\zh{青} (strokes 3-10).} A top horizontal; a second horizontal; a vertical down through them; a wide middle horizontal; then the lower box — its left side, then its top-and-right in one turning stroke that hooks at the base, then two short inner horizontals.

Nine pen lifts. \textbf{\zh{讠} finished before \zh{青}.}

Now the part worth stopping for. In \zh{谢}, both halves pointed at \textbf{meaning} — speech, body, inch. Here the right half does something else entirely.

\textbf{\zh{青} is said \emph{qīng}. The whole character is said \emph{qǐng}.}

Say those two aloud, one after the other. Same consonant, same rest of the syllable; only the pitch differs. \textbf{The right half is not telling you what the word means. It is telling you how to say it.} That is a \textbf{phonetic component} — the job \zh{尔} was doing inside \zh{你}, which you could only take on trust there. This time you can hear it. Once you can spot one you have a genuine reading strategy: meet an unknown character, find the half you recognise, and you often have a guess at the sound.

It is a guess and not a guarantee — the sound has drifted in plenty of characters over a few thousand years, and the tone in particular is often different, as it is here. But a guess beats nothing, and you will be right often.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{讠}, then \zh{青} — stopping between the two pieces
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{qīng}, then \textbf{qǐng} — the sound half, then the whole character
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{请} straight through
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is the sound half exactly right? (\textbf{Not quite} — the tone differs.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[qǐng]{\zh{请} — please, and after you}

\label{lesson:ZH-C11-qing}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{qǐng} — low and dipping, like \emph{hǎo} and \emph{wǒ}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\zh{请}} \emph{qǐng} — the word a dictionary will give you as \textbf{please}.

That translation is close enough to use and loose enough to mislead, so here is the more accurate version: \zh{请} is closer to \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I ask you to\textquotedblright{}}, \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I invite you to\textquotedblright{}}. Where English \emph{please} softens a demand, \zh{请} \textbf{hands the action over}.

Which is why it works \textbf{on its own}. Hold a door and say \zh{请} — that is \emph{after you}, \emph{go ahead}, \emph{be my guest}. Offer someone a seat and say \zh{请}. No other words needed, and none of them would be an apology for asking.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
English \emph{please} is a \textbf{softener}. You bolt it onto a request to take the edge off, and you can put it almost anywhere: \emph{please sit}, \emph{sit, please}, \emph{could you please sit}.

\zh{请} does not work like that. It comes \textbf{before the action it invites}, never bolted on after it — there is no Mandarin habit of tacking \zh{请} onto the end of a request the way English tacks on \emph{please}.

The consequence is practical, and it surprises learners: \textbf{Mandarin uses \zh{请} far less often than English uses please} — and with people you are close to it can sound distant rather than polite. Leaving it out is not rude the way dropping \emph{please} can be in English. Warmth in Mandarin is carried more by what you say and how you say it than by a single courtesy word.

So: use \zh{请} to hand something over or to invite. Do not reach for it every time you would say \emph{please} in English — you would sound stilted rather than polite.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{qǐng} on its own, as though holding a door open
  \item \textbf{qǐng}, then \textbf{xièxie} — the invitation, then the thanks
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does Mandarin use \zh{请} as often as English uses \emph{please}? (\textbf{No} — far less.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — after you}

\label{lesson:ZH-C11-practice}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{qǐng} — low and dipping.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Two people reach a door at the same time.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} \zh{请}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{qǐng} — after you.
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{B:} \zh{谢谢}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{xièxie} — thank you.
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} \zh{不谢}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{bú xiè} — you're welcome.
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{B:} \zh{再见}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{zàijiàn} — goodbye.
\end{quote}

Four lines, four words, and a complete small courtesy. Nobody in it asks for anything or explains anything, and it still works — which is most of what courtesy is.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — a component that predicts}]
Consider what the two halves of this chapter's character bought you.

\textbf{\zh{讠} on the left} told you the word was about speech before you knew what it meant — and it did the same in \zh{谢}. Two characters, one component, one reliable guess.

\textbf{\zh{青} on the right} told you roughly how to say it. You were told once before that a half could do this — \zh{尔}, on the right of \zh{你} — but you had to take it on trust, because \zh{尔} is \emph{ěr} and nothing in it sounds like \emph{nǐ}. Here you can hear it for yourself: \emph{qīng}, \emph{qǐng}.

So the claim made in passing back then is now one you can check: a Chinese character can carry \textbf{two kinds of hint at once}, one for what it means and one for how it is said. That is the single most useful thing to know about reading Chinese, and it is why the writing system is learnable at all rather than being thousands of unrelated pictures.

You will not always get both hints, and neither is a promise. But from here on, when you meet a character you do not know, you have something to do other than look it up: \textbf{find the half you recognise, and ask which job it is doing.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the whole exchange, both parts
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{qǐng}, \textbf{xièxie}, \textbf{bú xiè} — three courtesies in a row
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{请}, then \zh{谢} — and say what their left halves have in common
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which half of \zh{请} would help you guess its pronunciation? (\textbf{The right}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
